extracted.intended_audience: university/tertiary mathematics instructors and mathematics-education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for teaching, assessing, and supporting undergraduate (transition-to-proof) students in understanding, constructing, and validating mathematical proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand statement structure and content
rubrics_metrics.description: A student’s first job when given a statement to prove is to understand both the statement’s structure and its content; if informally stated they must ascertain which are the hypotheses and which is the conclusion (e.g., recognising 'whenever' as 'if').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professors should, at least initially, state theorems using familiar if-then and if-and-only-if forms to reduce linguistic confusion. Students should identify linguistic markers and separate hypotheses from conclusions before attempting a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpack definitions in the conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should unpack the conclusion by looking up and unpacking definitions of unfamiliar terms to understand what must be proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully unpacking definitions can indicate where to begin a proof. Failure to do this often leads students to focus wrongly on hypotheses and fail to reach the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-focusing on hypotheses (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students often initially focus on the hypotheses and deduce anything without moving toward the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should teach students to direct deductions toward the conclusion rather than wandering through consequences of hypotheses; provide tasks that require unpacking the conclusion first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret and use previous theorems and definitions correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must use relevant theorems/definitions correctly and verify that the hypotheses/conditions of those theorems are satisfied before applying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common errors include ignoring relevant hypotheses, applying converses that do not hold, treating named theorems as vague 'slogans', and incorrect substitutions (especially for compound variables). Instruction should emphasise checking applicability and precise substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have and use a repertoire of examples and non-examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing proofs requires persistence and a flexible concept image; students should generate examples and counterexamples to clarify concepts, judge conjectures, and disprove statements where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage example-generation (with reflection)—students who generate and reflect on examples make more progress. Ideal teaching examples are 'only just' examples and non-examples are 'very nearly' examples. Warn against memorisation and of producing trivially related examples (e.g., just translates). Require students to check that examples satisfy relevant definitions and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select helpful representations when proving
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should know which symbolic or graphical representations make particular properties transparent and should move flexibly between representations when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some representations make certain features easy to see (transparent) and others obscure (opaque). Instructors should model and provide practice choosing representations (e.g., linear transformations vs matrices). Note conversion can be cognitively complex and asymmetric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring relevant factual knowledge to mind when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must be able to access and deploy useful facts, formulas, definitions, and theorems at appropriate times while solving problems and constructing proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research shows students may possess resources but fail to recognise their relevance. Teaching should include tasks and practice that encourage noticing and retrieving varied approaches rather than mimicking worked examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know which theorems are important and when to use them
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should learn to recognise fundamental and useful theorems and to bring them to bear on appropriate problems (meta-mathematical ability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop experience so students know which results are 'one of the first things you turn to'. Teach both semantic reasoning (use examples to gain insight then translate to definitions/theorems) and syntactic reasoning (use the statement and logical structure), and discuss when each is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish semantic and syntactic reasoning strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Two reasoning strategies: semantic (using examples/meaning to gain insight and then formalise) and syntactic (structuring proofs from formal statements and logical inferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both strategies are useful; syntactic approaches may be necessary when concepts lack pictorial representations, but can fail if syntactic representations are very complex. Instruction should expose students to both and help them decide which approach fits the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and check proofs (proof validation skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: An integral skill is the ability to tell whether an argument is correct: checking step-by-step that each assertion follows, that steps are logical, and that computations are complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice with evaluating purported proofs (including student-generated proofs) improves accuracy; validation activities in groups can improve proof writing. Inexperienced readers (students and some teachers) may misidentify nonproofs as proofs—explicit training is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make expectations clear when asking students to produce proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers must be explicit about what is meant by terms like 'explain', 'demonstrate', 'show', 'justify', and 'prove' because students respond differently and may produce travelogues or redundant explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether a task requires explanation (descriptive), argumentation (semantic content matters), or proof (structure + content determine truth). Model precise mathematical language (e.g., quantifiers) and provide explicit rubrics for required formality and detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be exemplary and consistent in the use of quantifiers and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should model strict and correct usage of quantification and notation to avoid confusing students with inconsistent or implicit quantifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show textbooks and teachers sometimes vary quantifier usage; teachers should avoid informal shorthand they reject from students and consistently demonstrate correct formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use transition-to-proof (bridge) course structure effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses intended to help students move from computational to proof-based mathematics typically include logic, direct/indirect proofs, sets, relations, functions, induction, and practice proving in specific areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such courses are often small (15–40 students) and may employ small-group learning, presentations, or mixed methods. Evidence on effectiveness is limited but some studies show improved outcomes; course design should emphasise practice in constructing proofs rather than mere formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster proving in a community of practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning by jointly constructing mathematics (definitions, conjectures, proofs) with teacher orchestration can develop students' abilities to justify statements and participate in axiomatisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher acts as expert orchestrator via carefully developed questions/tasks, use of tools (e.g., dynamic geometry), and class management. This approach provides experience students can later use in teaching contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Moore Method or modified inquiry approaches where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods where students prove/theorise from given definitions/theorems with minimal help (Moore Method), or co-construct proofs with instructor prompts, can accelerate independent proving skills in small classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods work best in small groups and require careful structuring and critique. Co-construction is slow but can improve students' reflective abilities; teachers should balance pace and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement the method of scientific debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage a classroom mathematical community where students propose conjectures, discuss proofs/refutations/counterexamples, and the class collectively decides which conjectures become theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For success, renegotiate the didactic contract so students accept responsibilities, the teacher refrains from revealing opinions, allows time for argument development, and encourages maximum participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generic (transparent pseudo-) proofs pedagogically
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a carefully chosen particular case (generic example) that reveals the general argument (e.g., Gauss's n=100 sum trick) to help students engage with the main ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk: students may not grasp the generic nature. To mitigate, follow with requiring students to write the general proof or explicitly discuss how the particular case generalises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure mathematical proofs in multi-level form
rubrics_metrics.description: Present proofs on levels (top-down): top level gives main ideas succinctly; middle levels elaborate; bottom level contains full technical detail—this can help communicate main ideas while preserving rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured proofs to present higher-level ideas and have students fill in lower levels, or ask students to find structure in textbook proofs. Empirical evidence for ease-of-comprehension is limited but it's a recommended pedagogical strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make use of writing-to-learn exercises about proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students critique fictional student dialogues and written proofs, identify errors, judge understanding, and justify reactions as a way to deepen proof comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sample scenarios, scaffolding instructions for thoughtful responses, and grading guidance. Such exercises can reveal students' conceptual understanding and reasoning about proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess proof comprehension with varied question types
rubrics_metrics.description: Use comprehension tasks where students are given a proof from class and must answer questions: identify method of proof, definitions, justificable assumptions, fill gaps, or analyse effects of changing conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tests motivate understanding rather than rote reproduction; prepare students with similar homework tasks. Students prefer comprehension tasks to simple reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use video and multimedia resources to teach proof moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Videos of students constructing proofs can be used for reflection; three significant 'moments' are identified: obtaining a key idea, finding the technical handle to formalise it, and producing the final standard-form proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use videos to prompt discussion and reflection (best in small classes). e-Proofs (line-by-line explanations with structural breakdowns) allow students to replay sections. Tools like ExPOUND aim to support authoring such resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide research-based resources (booklets/DVDs) for instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: Short booklets and DVDs combining research findings, examples of student responses, suggested practices, and references help instructors translate research into pedagogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute such materials to faculty; they include topics such as proof by example/counterexample, induction, contradiction, concept images, and distinctions between semantic/syntactic reasoning.
